content: Technology facilitates the transmission of critical information regarding a patient’s condition to the receiving healthcare facility. This communication enables the hospital to prepare the necessary resources in advance, ensuring they are ready to meet the patient’s needs upon arrival. Essential details to be conveyed include the mechanism and nature of the injury, the number of victims, their condition during transport, and the estimated time of arrival at the hospital. Wireless communication systems allow for real-time medical oversight of ambulance crews, enhancing the quality of care. For instance, a medical director or supervisor can monitor communications between the crew and the healthcare facility. In most cases, the medical director observes to ensure care is proceeding appropriately. However, they may also provide specific treatment instructions or intervene to alter the care plan if necessary. For example, the medical director might redirect an ambulance to a more suitable facility based on the patient’s needs. To ensure consistent and competent medical oversight, it is preferable for a single facility, typically a local or regional hospital, to manage wireless communications between ambulances and medical directors within the area. Communication networks can also be leveraged to improve prehospital care training through distance education, made increasingly feasible by satellite communication technology, which maintains clear signals even in remote locations. Many countries have implemented nationwide emergency telephone numbers to streamline access to emergency services. However, the specific number varies by country, and no single number is universally recognized. Automatic location identification is more reliable with landlines than wireless communication, which poses challenges for call localization, even in high-income countries. Centralized dispatch centers have proven to be more efficient and cost-effective than multiple independent centers. For example, replacing 27 dispatch centers with a single center reduced costs, improved efficiency, and allowed major event alerts to be issued in under a minute. Such centers handle a high volume of calls daily, though many are false alarms. Medical directors and field supervisors play a crucial role in ensuring the quality of prehospital care. They can monitor team performance, review written reports, and provide feedback to address issues. Critical incident reviews and morbidity and mortality reviews are valuable tools for analyzing errors and improving care. These reviews should focus on identifying root causes and systemic issues rather than assigning blame, fostering a culture of learning and improvement. Outcome studies, which track the clinical outcomes of specific conditions, can help assess the effectiveness of prehospital systems. These studies, combined with data on injury incidence and care processes, provide insights into whether the system is achieving its goals of saving lives and reducing long-term disability. Continuing education is vital for maintaining the skills and knowledge of prehospital providers, especially for infrequently used skills. While there is no standard frequency for such education, it is essential to ensure providers remain competent. Educational materials are often available at little or no cost, though they are predominantly in English. Discipline is critical in prehospital trauma care. Supervisors and medical directors must have the authority to enforce standards and take corrective action when necessary. This may involve clarifying expectations, providing remedial education, or, in severe cases, suspending or terminating a provider’s patient care privileges. Prehospital care systems must be designed to function efficiently on a daily basis to prepare for mass casualty events. Improvements in prehospital care should be accompanied by enhancements in facility-based trauma care to ensure patients receive adequate treatment upon arrival. Collaborative efforts, such as the Essential Trauma Care Project, have identified core services and resources necessary for effective trauma care, which have been used to assess needs in various countries. Advanced prehospital trauma care, or advanced life support (ALS), involves sophisticated interventions to sustain life. While costly, ALS is typically available in high-income countries and provided by specialized ambulances staffed by highly trained professionals, often including physicians in some regions.
